title: Remove, dismantle and install drive train components of agricultural equipment

lessons.title: Knowing the drive train and getting ready safely
lessons.html:
What is the drive train?

The drive train takes power from the engine to the wheels. On a farm tractor it has these main parts:

  • Clutch – connects and disconnects the engine from the gearbox.
  • Gearbox (transmission) – gives different speeds and reverse.
  • Differential – lets the back wheels turn at different speeds in a corner.
  • Final drives – the last gears that turn the axles and wheels.
  • Drive shafts and universal joints – carry power, for example to the front axle on a 4x4 tractor.
  • PTO (power take-off) – drives implements like a slasher or a pump.

Before you start

Drive train parts are heavy. A clutch or a final drive can weigh far more than one person can lift. Plan the job with your supervisor first.

  1. Read the workshop manual for that model. Note the steps and the torque values.
  2. Park the tractor on a flat, hard floor. Put it in neutral, pull the handbrake and switch off. Take the key out.
  3. Disconnect the battery negative cable so nobody can start it.
  4. Put chocks in front of and behind the wheels.
  5. Get the right tools: spanners, sockets, torque wrench, pullers, drip trays, a trolley jack and axle stands, and a hoist or crane if needed.
  6. Wear overalls, safety boots, gloves and safety glasses.

Never do this

  • Never work under a tractor held up only by a jack. Always use axle stands or proper blocks.
  • Never stand under a part hanging from a hoist.
  • Never lift a heavy part alone. Ask for help or use lifting gear.

The Occupational Health and Safety Act 85 of 1993 says your employer must give you safe tools and training, and you must follow the safety rules. If you are not sure, stop and ask.

lessons.title: Removing and dismantling drive train parts
lessons.html:
Draining oil first

Most drive train parts sit in oil. Put a drip tray under the drain plug, take the plug out and let the oil run out. Keep used oil in a closed drum for recycling. Never pour it onto the ground or into a drain or river.

Removing a part step by step

  1. Clean the outside of the part with a brush or degreaser so dirt does not fall inside.
  2. Take photos or make notes of where pipes, wires and linkages go.
  3. Disconnect linkages, hoses and wires. Put tags on them.
  4. Support the part with a jack, a stand or a hoist before you take out the last bolts.
  5. Undo the bolts in a cross pattern, a little at a time.
  6. Slide the part out straight. Do not force it or hit it with a steel hammer. Use a soft hammer if it is stuck.

Dismantling on the bench

Put the part on a clean bench. Take it apart in the order the manual shows. Lay the pieces out in a row in the same order. Keep small parts like shims, circlips and bearings in labelled containers.

Look at each part and report what you see:

  • Gears with chipped, cracked or worn teeth.
  • Bearings that are rough, loose or blue from heat.
  • Seals that are hard, cracked or leaking.
  • Splines that are worn or twisted.
  • Metal pieces in the oil – this means something is wearing badly.

Write down every damaged part on the job card so your supervisor can order new parts. Use the part numbers from the manual or the old part.

lessons.title: Installing drive train parts and testing
lessons.html:
Getting ready to install

Everything must be clean before it goes back. Wash parts in clean solvent and let them dry. Clean the old gasket off the faces with a scraper, but do not scratch the metal.

  • Fit new seals, gaskets and O-rings. Never reuse an old seal.
  • Put a thin film of clean oil on bearings and gears.
  • Put back the same shims in the same place, unless the manual says to measure and change them.

Installing step by step

  1. Lift the part with the hoist or jack and line it up carefully.
  2. Slide it in straight. Turn the shaft a little so the splines line up. Never pull it in with the bolts.
  3. Fit the bolts by hand first.
  4. Tighten the bolts in a cross pattern with the torque wrench to the value in the manual.
  5. Connect the linkages, hoses and wires using your tags and photos.
  6. Put in the drain plug and fill with the correct oil to the right level. Use the oil type in the manual.

Testing the job

Reconnect the battery. Start the tractor with the wheels still chocked and check:

  • There are no oil leaks.
  • The clutch works and the gears go in smoothly.
  • There are no strange noises, grinding or knocking.

Then do a short, slow test drive in a safe place with your supervisor. Check the oil level again after the test. Clean the work area, put tools away and fill in the job card.

Key points

  • Plan the job, read the manual and switch off and disconnect the battery first.
  • Always support the tractor on axle stands and use lifting gear for heavy parts.
  • Keep parts in order and label them when you take them apart.
  • Fit new seals and tighten bolts to the manual torque.
  • Test for leaks and noises before the tractor goes back to work.
